records.source: וַיְדַבֵּ֧ר יְהוָ֛ה אֶל־מֹשֶׁ֥ה וְאֶֽל־אַהֲרֹ֖ן לֵאמֹ֥ר אֲלֵהֶֽם׃
records.gloss: And spoke Yahweh to Moses and to Aaron, saying to them,
pieces: {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} spoke to Moses and Aaron. He said to them,

L.1: And {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} spoke to Moses and to Aaron, saying to them,

R.1: {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} said to Moses and Aaron,

decisions.choice: to Moses and to Aaron: the instruction is given to both, to pass on to Israel
decisions.reason: God speaks to Aaron as well as Moses here, as again in 13:1, 14:33 and 15:1, the chapters on clean and unclean. In 10:10-11 the priests were charged to distinguish between the unclean and the clean and to teach Israel the statutes; this chapter gives them the first of those teachings.

decisions.choice: He said to them / said to
decisions.reason: The formula follows the settled wording of 1:1, with "to them" because two people are addressed.

records.heading: Clean and unclean animals

records.source: דַּבְּר֛וּ אֶל־בְּנֵ֥י יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל לֵאמֹ֑ר זֹ֤את הַֽחַיָּה֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר תֹּאכְל֔וּ מִכָּל־הַבְּהֵמָ֖ה אֲשֶׁ֥ר עַל־הָאָֽרֶץ׃
records.gloss: Speak to [the] sons of Israel, saying, this [is] the living creature which you will eat from every animal which [is] on the earth.
pieces: "Speak to the {{gender:Israelites|sons of Israel}} and tell them: 'Of all the animals that live on land, these are the creatures you may eat.

L.2: "Speak to the {{gender:children|sons}} of Israel, saying, 'This [is] the living creature that you may eat out of all the animals that [are] on the earth:

R.2: "Tell the {{gender:Israelites|sons of Israel}}: 'Here are the land animals that you may eat.

decisions.choice: living creature ... animal: any living land creature, wild or tame
decisions.reason: The first word is the general word for a living creature. The second can mean domestic livestock, but here it covers all the larger land animals "on the earth", since the list in Deuteronomy 14:4-5 includes the deer and the wild goat. The chapter moves from land animals (verses 2-8) to water creatures (9-12), birds (13-19), winged swarming creatures (20-23) and creatures that swarm on the ground (29-31, 41-43), roughly the order of creation in Genesis 1:20-25.

decisions.choice: you will eat: you may eat; the verb gives permission
decisions.reason: The Hebrew future is used here for what is allowed. The chapter is not a list of what must be eaten but of what is permitted and what is forbidden.

decisions.choice: that live on land / land animals
decisions.reason: "On the earth" means on dry land as opposed to the waters of verse 9. Balanced and Readable say "land" to make that plain.

records.source: כֹּ֣ל׀מַפְרֶ֣סֶת פַּרְסָ֗ה וְשֹׁסַ֤עַת שֶׁ֨סַע֙ פְּרָסֹ֔ת מַעֲלַ֥ת גֵּרָ֖ה בַּבְּהֵמָ֑ה אֹתָ֖הּ תֹּאכֵֽלוּ׃
records.gloss: Every [one which] divides [a] hoof and cleaves [a] cleft of hooves, bringing up cud among the animals, it you will eat.
pieces: You may eat any animal that both chews the cud and has hooves split fully in two.

L.3: Any that divides the hoof and is split [with] a cleft of hooves, [and] brings up the cud, among the animals, it you may eat.

R.3: You may eat any animal that chews the cud and also has hooves that are split into two parts.

decisions.choice: divides the hoof and is split with a cleft: the hoof is split completely into two toes
decisions.reason: Two phrases say the same thing: the hoof is divided, and the split goes all the way through. Cattle, sheep, goats and deer have such hooves; the horse, with a single solid hoof, does not.

decisions.choice: brings up the cud: chews again food brought back up from the stomach
decisions.reason: The cud is food that an animal such as a cow or a sheep swallows, brings up again and chews a second time. An animal that is to be eaten must have both signs, the split hoof and the chewing of the cud; verses 4-7 give examples of animals with only one.

decisions.choice: chews the cud
decisions.reason: Literal keeps "brings up the cud". Balanced and Readable use the usual expression "chews the cud".

records.source: אַ֤ךְ אֶת־זֶה֙ לֹ֣א תֹֽאכְל֔וּ מִֽמַּעֲלֵי֙ הַגֵּרָ֔ה וּמִמַּפְרִיסֵ֖י הַפַּרְסָ֑ה אֶֽת־הַ֠גָּמָל כִּֽי־מַעֲלֵ֨ה גֵרָ֜ה ה֗וּא וּפַרְסָה֙ אֵינֶ֣נּוּ מַפְרִ֔יס טָמֵ֥א ה֖וּא לָכֶֽם׃
records.gloss: Nevertheless this you must not eat, from [those which] bring up the cud and from [those which] divide the hoof: the camel, for bringing up cud [is] it, and [a] hoof not it divides; unclean [is] it to you.
pieces: Yet you must not eat these, even though they chew the cud or have split hooves: the camel, because it chews the cud but its hoof is not split. It is unclean for you.

L.4: Nevertheless, these you shall not eat, from those that bring up the cud or from those that divide the hoof: the camel, for it brings up the cud, but the hoof it does not divide; it [is] unclean to you.

R.4: But do not eat the animals that have only one of the two signs. The camel chews the cud, but its hoof is not split, so it is unclean for you.

decisions.choice: unclean: ritually impure, unfit to eat and kept apart from what is holy
decisions.reason: Unclean is not the same as dirty or sinful. It is a state that God's law assigns to certain animals, bodies and objects, and the opposite of it is clean (verse 47). Leviticus sets two pairs side by side, holy and common, unclean and clean (10:10). An unclean person may not eat holy food or come near the sanctuary (7:20-21; 12:4) until made clean again. Some animals are unclean "to you": they are forbidden as food to Israel, and their dead bodies make a person unclean (verses 8, 24-28). Living camels and donkeys could still be ridden and handled. Peter's vision in Acts 10:9-16 and Jesus' words in Mark 7:19 later set aside these food laws for the followers of Jesus.

decisions.choice: the camel: it chews the cud, but its foot is not a split hoof
decisions.reason: A camel's foot has two toes resting on a broad, soft pad, not two separate hard hooves like those of cattle. So it has only one of the two signs.

decisions.choice: unclean for you
decisions.reason: "To you" means as far as you are concerned, for your eating. Balanced says "for you".

records.source: וְאֶת־הַשָּׁפָ֗ן כִּֽי־מַעֲלֵ֤ה גֵרָה֙ ה֔וּא וּפַרְסָ֖ה לֹ֣א יַפְרִ֑יס טָמֵ֥א ה֖וּא לָכֶֽם׃
records.gloss: And the rock badger, for bringing up cud [is] it, and [a] hoof not it divides; unclean [is] it to you.
pieces: The rock badger chews the cud, but its hoof is not split; it is unclean for you.

L.5: And the rock badger, for it brings up the cud, but the hoof it does not divide; it [is] unclean to you.

R.5: The rock badger chews the cud, but its feet do not have split hooves. So it is unclean for you.

decisions.choice: rock badger: probably the rock hyrax, a small animal that lives among rocks
decisions.reason: The animal is said to live among the rocks (Psalm 104:18; Proverbs 30:26). This fits the rock hyrax, a small furry animal about the size of a rabbit that is common in the rocky places of the land, and the identification is widely accepted, though not certain. It is not a true badger.

decisions.choice: brings up the cud: the animal looks as if it is chewing the cud
decisions.reason: The hyrax and the hare (verse 6) do not have the several stomachs of cattle and sheep. But they move their jaws constantly as if chewing, and the hare eats some of its own droppings to digest them again. The law describes the animals as an observer sees them.

records.source: וְאֶת־הָאַרְנֶ֗בֶת כִּֽי־מַעֲלַ֤ת גֵּרָה֙ הִ֔וא וּפַרְסָ֖ה לֹ֣א הִפְרִ֑יסָה טְמֵאָ֥ה הִ֖וא לָכֶֽם׃
records.gloss: And the hare, for bringing up cud [is] it, and [a] hoof not it divides; unclean [is] it to you.
pieces: The hare also chews the cud, but its hoof is not split; it is unclean for you.

L.6: And the hare, for it brings up the cud, but the hoof it does not divide; it [is] unclean to you.

R.6: The hare also chews the cud, but it does not have split hooves. So it is unclean for you.

decisions.choice: the hare: the wild hare of the land
decisions.reason: The word is the usual one for the hare. The rabbit is not native to the land. On "brings up the cud" see verse 5.

records.source: וְאֶת־הַ֠חֲזִיר כִּֽי־מַפְרִ֨יס פַּרְסָ֜ה ה֗וּא וְשֹׁסַ֥ע שֶׁ֨סַע֙ פַּרְסָ֔ה וְה֖וּא גֵּרָ֣ה לֹֽא־יִגָּ֑ר טָמֵ֥א ה֖וּא לָכֶֽם׃
records.gloss: And the pig, for dividing [a] hoof [is] it and cleaving [a] cleft of [a] hoof, and it cud not it chews; unclean [is] it to you.
pieces: The pig has hooves split fully in two, but it does not chew the cud; it is unclean for you.

L.7: And the pig, for it divides the hoof and is split [with] a cleft of the hoof, but it does not chew the cud; it [is] unclean to you.

R.7: The pig has split hooves, but it does not chew the cud. So it is unclean for you.

decisions.choice: the pig: the example of an animal with split hooves that does not chew the cud
decisions.reason: The pig is the one animal named with the opposite lack to the camel, rock badger and hare. Later Scripture treats eating pork as a mark of turning away from God (Isaiah 65:4; 66:17), and in the time of the Maccabees Jews chose death rather than eat it.

decisions.choice: chew: a different verb from "bring up", meaning to chew the cud
decisions.reason: Here the verb is not "bring up" but one that means to drag or chew; with "cud" it means the same thing.

records.source: מִבְּשָׂרָם֙ לֹ֣א תֹאכֵ֔לוּ וּבְנִבְלָתָ֖ם לֹ֣א תִגָּ֑עוּ טְמֵאִ֥ים הֵ֖ם לָכֶֽם׃
records.gloss: From their meat not you must eat, and their carcass not you will touch; unclean [are] they to you.
pieces: Do not eat any of their meat, and do not touch them when they are dead. They are unclean for you.

L.8: Of their meat you shall not eat, and their carcass you shall not touch; they [are] unclean to you.

R.8: Do not eat their meat. Do not touch their bodies after they have died. They are unclean for you.

decisions.choice: carcass: the dead body of an animal
decisions.reason: The word is used for the body of an animal that has died or been killed, not slaughtered for food. The ban on touching concerns these animals when dead, not the living camel or donkey.

decisions.choice: you shall not touch: avoid contact with their dead bodies, which makes a person unclean
decisions.reason: Verses 24-28 show what follows if someone does touch such a carcass: the person is unclean until evening and must wash. So this is a warning to avoid becoming unclean, not a crime with a penalty.

decisions.choice: when they are dead / after they have died
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "when they are dead" for "their carcass", so that the reader does not take it as a ban on touching a living animal.

records.source: אֶת־זֶה֙ תֹּֽאכְל֔וּ מִכֹּ֖ל אֲשֶׁ֣ר בַּמָּ֑יִם כֹּ֣ל אֲשֶׁר־לוֹ֩ סְנַפִּ֨יר וְקַשְׂקֶ֜שֶׂת בַּמַּ֗יִם בַּיַּמִּ֛ים וּבַנְּחָלִ֖ים אֹתָ֥ם תֹּאכֵֽלוּ׃
records.gloss: This you will eat from all which [is] in the waters: all which [belongs] to it fin and scale in the waters, in the seas and in the streams, them you will eat.
pieces: These are the water creatures you may eat: whatever has fins and scales, whether it lives in the seas or in the streams.

L.9: This you may eat of all that [are] in the waters: everything that has fin and scale in the waters, in the seas and in the streams, them you may eat.

R.9: You may eat water animals that have fins and scales. It does not matter whether they live in the sea or in a river.

decisions.choice: fin and scale: the two marks of fish that may be eaten
decisions.reason: As with land animals, a water creature must have both marks. Most fish have both; eels, catfish, shellfish and other sea creatures do not (verse 10).

decisions.choice: streams: river valleys and the streams that run in them, including those that flow only in the rainy season
decisions.reason: The word is used of a valley with a stream, and of the stream itself. With "seas" it covers both salt water and fresh.

records.source: וְכֹל֩ אֲשֶׁ֨ר אֵֽין־ל֜וֹ סְנַפִּ֣יר וְקַשְׂקֶ֗שֶׂת בַּיַּמִּים֙ וּבַנְּחָלִ֔ים מִכֹּל֙ שֶׁ֣רֶץ הַמַּ֔יִם וּמִכֹּ֛ל נֶ֥פֶשׁ הַחַיָּ֖ה אֲשֶׁ֣ר בַּמָּ֑יִם שֶׁ֥קֶץ הֵ֖ם לָכֶֽם׃
records.gloss: And all which there [belongs] not to it fin and scale in the seas and in the streams, of every swarming thing of the waters and of every living creature which [is] in the waters, detestable [are] they to you.
pieces: But anything in the seas or streams without fins and scales, whether it is one of the small creatures that swarm in the water or any other living thing there, is to be detestable to you.

L.10: But all that does not have fin and scale in the seas and in the streams, of every swarming thing of the waters and of every living creature that [is] in the waters, they [are] detestable to you.

R.10: But you must think of all other water animals as disgusting. These are the ones without fins and scales, both the small ones that swarm in the water and all the others.

decisions.choice: detestable: to be regarded with loathing and kept at a distance
decisions.reason: This noun and the verb from the same root, "detest" (verses 11, 13, 43), are used in this chapter for creatures that must not be eaten: water creatures without fins and scales, the birds of verses 13-19, winged swarming creatures and creatures that swarm on the ground. It is a different word from the one used for the "detestable" acts of 18:22, though Deuteronomy 14:3 uses that other word for the unclean foods. A related noun is used of idols (1 Kings 11:5). Israel is to share God's verdict on these creatures and treat them as repulsive.

decisions.choice: swarming thing: a small creature that appears in great numbers
decisions.reason: The word is used of creatures that teem and multiply, as in Genesis 1:20, "Let the waters swarm with swarms of living creatures". It covers small creatures of the water, winged insects (verse 20) and small creatures that swarm on the ground (verses 29, 41).

decisions.choice: disgusting
decisions.reason: Readable says "disgusting" for "detestable" throughout the chapter, a word a young reader knows.

records.source: וְשֶׁ֖קֶץ יִהְי֣וּ לָכֶ֑ם מִבְּשָׂרָם֙ לֹ֣א תֹאכֵ֔לוּ וְאֶת־נִבְלָתָ֖ם תְּשַׁקֵּֽצוּ׃
records.gloss: And detestable they will be to you; from their meat not you must eat, and their carcass you will detest.
pieces: They are to remain detestable to you. Do not eat their meat, and treat their dead bodies as detestable.

L.11: And they shall be detestable to you; of their meat you shall not eat, and their carcass you shall detest.

R.11: They must stay disgusting to you. Do not eat their meat, and think of their dead bodies as disgusting.

decisions.choice: you shall detest: treat as detestable, keep away from
decisions.reason: The verb means to regard and treat something as detestable. Unlike the land animals of verse 8, nothing is said here about uncleanness from touching these dead bodies; the stress is on refusing them as food. See verse 10.

records.source: כֹּ֣ל אֲשֶׁ֥ר אֵֽין־ל֛וֹ סְנַפִּ֥יר וְקַשְׂקֶ֖שֶׂת בַּמָּ֑יִם שֶׁ֥קֶץ ה֖וּא לָכֶֽם׃
records.gloss: All which there [belongs] not to it fin and scale in the waters, detestable [is] it to you.
pieces: Whatever lives in the water without fins and scales is to be detestable to you.

L.12: All that does not have fin and scale in the waters, it [is] detestable to you.

R.12: Any water animal without fins and scales is disgusting to you.

decisions.choice: detestable: the rule of verses 9-11 is repeated as a summary
decisions.reason: The repetition closes the section on water creatures. See verse 10.

records.source: וְאֶת־אֵ֨לֶּה֙ תְּשַׁקְּצ֣וּ מִן־הָע֔וֹף לֹ֥א יֵאָכְל֖וּ שֶׁ֣קֶץ הֵ֑ם אֶת־הַנֶּ֨שֶׁר֙ וְאֶת־הַפֶּ֔רֶס וְאֵ֖ת הָעָזְנִיָּֽה׃
records.gloss: And these you will detest from the birds; not they will be eaten; detestable [are] they: the eagle, and the bearded vulture, and the black vulture,
pieces: Among the birds, these are the ones you are to detest. They must not be eaten, because they are detestable: the eagle, the bearded vulture, the black vulture,

L.13: And these you shall detest among the birds; they shall not be eaten; they [are] detestable: the eagle, and the bearded vulture, and the black vulture,

R.13: Here are the birds that you must think of as disgusting. Do not eat them: the eagle, the bearded vulture, the black vulture,

decisions.choice: the birds of verses 13-19: names whose exact identity is often uncertain
decisions.reason: The list gives names, not marks as for land animals and fish. Many of the names occur only here and in the parallel list in Deuteronomy 14:12-18, so their identification rests on context, ancient versions and the meaning of the words. Most of those that can be identified are birds of prey, carrion eaters, or birds of marsh and ruin, which may explain why they are forbidden. The names in this translation are the best identifications, not certainties.

decisions.choice: eagle: a large bird of prey, possibly the griffon vulture
decisions.reason: The word is usually the eagle, but it can include the great vultures: Micah 1:16 speaks of baldness like that of this bird, which fits the griffon vulture's bare head.

decisions.choice: the list runs on to verse 19
decisions.reason: The list of birds is one sentence in Hebrew from verse 13 to verse 19, so Literal and Balanced end verses 13-18 with a comma.

records.source: וְאֶת־הַ֨דָּאָ֔ה וְאֶת־הָאַיָּ֖ה לְמִינָֽהּ׃
records.gloss: and the red kite, and the black kite after its kind,
pieces: the red kite, the various kinds of black kite,

L.14: and the red kite, and the black kite after its kind,

R.14: the red kite, all kinds of black kites,

decisions.choice: red kite, black kite: birds of prey that hunt and scavenge
decisions.reason: The first name probably comes from a verb for swooping; Deuteronomy 14:13 has a similar name in its place. The second is a keen-sighted bird of prey (Job 28:7). Both are probably kites, but this is not certain.

decisions.choice: after its kind: including all the birds of that kind
decisions.reason: The phrase, as in Genesis 1:11-25, widens the name to the whole group of related birds.

records.source: אֵ֥ת כָּל־עֹרֵ֖ב לְמִינֽוֹ׃
records.gloss: every raven after its kind,
pieces: every kind of raven,

R.15: all kinds of ravens and crows,

decisions.choice: raven: the raven and the birds related to it
decisions.reason: The raven is a well-known bird (Genesis 8:7; 1 Kings 17:4-6). "After its kind" includes the crows.

decisions.choice: ravens and crows
decisions.reason: Readable names the crow, the best-known bird of the raven's kind.

records.source: וְאֵת֙ בַּ֣ת הַֽיַּעֲנָ֔ה וְאֶת־הַתַּחְמָ֖ס וְאֶת־הַשָּׁ֑חַף וְאֶת־הַנֵּ֖ץ לְמִינֵֽהוּ׃
records.gloss: and the daughter of the ostrich, and the screech owl, and the gull, and the falcon after its kind,
pieces: the ostrich, the screech owl, the gull, the various kinds of falcon,

L.16: and the ostrich, and the screech owl, and the gull, and the falcon after its kind,

R.16: the ostrich, the screech owl, the seagull, all kinds of falcons,

decisions.choice: the ostrich: literally "the daughter of the desert bird", probably the ostrich
decisions.reason: The phrase is used of a bird of the desert and of ruins, known for its cry (Job 30:29; Isaiah 13:21; Micah 1:8). The ostrich fits, though some take it as a large owl.

decisions.choice: screech owl, gull, falcon: uncertain identifications
decisions.reason: The first name may come from a verb for violence or for robbing; the second from a word for thin or lean; the third, a bird of prey, is named in Job 39:26 for flying south. These identifications are probable, not certain.

records.source: וְאֶת־הַכּ֥וֹס וְאֶת־הַשָּׁלָ֖ךְ וְאֶת־הַיַּנְשֽׁוּף׃
records.gloss: and the little owl, and the cormorant, and the great owl,
pieces: the little owl, the cormorant, the eagle owl,

L.17: and the little owl, and the cormorant, and the eagle owl,

R.17: the little owl, the cormorant, the eagle owl,

decisions.choice: little owl, cormorant, eagle owl: probable identifications
decisions.reason: The first is an owl of ruins (Psalm 102:7). The second comes from a verb meaning to throw down, which fits a bird that plunges after fish. The third lives in ruined places (Isaiah 34:11) and is probably a large owl. None of these is certain.

records.source: וְאֶת־הַתִּנְשֶׁ֥מֶת וְאֶת־הַקָּאָ֖ת וְאֶת־הָרָחָֽם׃
records.gloss: and the barn owl, and the desert owl, and the Egyptian vulture,
pieces: the barn owl, the desert owl, the carrion vulture,

L.18: and the barn owl, and the desert owl, and the carrion vulture,

R.18: the barn owl, the desert owl, the vulture,

decisions.choice: barn owl, desert owl, carrion vulture: probable identifications
decisions.reason: The first name is the same word as the last of the creatures in verse 30, so it may come from a verb for breathing or hissing. The second lives in deserts and ruins (Psalm 102:7; Isaiah 34:11; Zephaniah 2:14). The third comes from a root for tenderness, and is probably the small white Egyptian vulture, which feeds on carrion.

records.source: וְאֵת֙ הַחֲסִידָ֔ה הָאֲנָפָ֖ה לְמִינָ֑הּ וְאֶת־הַדּוּכִיפַ֖ת וְאֶת־הָעֲטַלֵּֽף׃
records.gloss: and the stork, the heron after its kind, and the hoopoe, and the bat.
pieces: the stork, the various kinds of heron, the hoopoe and the bat.

L.19: and the stork, the heron after its kind, and the hoopoe, and the bat.

R.19: the stork, all kinds of herons, the hoopoe and the bat.

decisions.choice: stork, heron, hoopoe: birds known from their habits
decisions.reason: The stork nests in trees and migrates (Psalm 104:17; Jeremiah 8:7). The heron is less certain. The hoopoe is a crested bird that probes the ground and dung for insects.

decisions.choice: the bat: a flying creature, though not a bird
decisions.reason: The word translated "birds" in verse 13 means flying creatures in general, so the bat can be listed with them (compare Isaiah 2:20).

records.gloss: Every swarming thing of the flying [kind] which walks on four, detestable [is] it to you.
pieces: Any swarming creature with wings that also walks on all fours is to be detestable to you.

L.20: Every swarming thing that flies, that goes on four [legs], it [is] detestable to you.

R.20: Insects with wings that crawl about on their legs are disgusting to you.

decisions.choice: goes on four: moves along on its legs like a four-footed animal
decisions.reason: Insects have six legs, so "on four" is not a count. It describes a creature that walks along with its body level, as four-footed animals do, rather than standing upright like a bird. The flying swarming things are winged insects.

decisions.choice: crawl about on their legs
decisions.reason: Readable explains "on all fours" rather than giving a number of legs that does not fit insects.

records.source: אַ֤ךְ אֶת־זֶה֙ תֹּֽאכְל֔וּ מִכֹּל֙ שֶׁ֣רֶץ הָע֔וֹף הַהֹלֵ֖ךְ עַל־אַרְבַּ֑ע אֲשֶׁר־ל֤וֹ כְרָעַ֨יִם֙ מִמַּ֣עַל לְרַגְלָ֔יו לְנַתֵּ֥ר בָּהֵ֖ן עַל־הָאָֽרֶץ׃
records.gloss: Nevertheless this you will eat from every swarming thing of the flying [kind] which walks on four: which [belong] to it legs from above its feet to hop with them on the ground.
pieces: But you may eat some of the winged swarming creatures that walk on all fours: those that have a pair of long legs above their feet for hopping across the ground.

L.21: Nevertheless, this you may eat of every swarming thing that flies, that goes on four [legs]: those that have legs above their feet with which to leap on the ground.

R.21: But you may eat some of these insects. You may eat the ones that have long back legs for jumping.

decisions.choice: which have: the reading tradition, rather than the written "which not"
decisions.reason: The consonants written in the text spell "not", but the Masoretic reading tradition, which the Westminster Leningrad Codex follows, reads "to it", that is, "which have". The two words sound the same in Hebrew. Only "which have" makes sense with the leaping legs that follow.

decisions.choice: legs above their feet to leap with: the long jumping hind legs of locusts and grasshoppers
decisions.reason: The word for these legs is used of the hind legs or shanks of an animal (Exodus 12:9). Insects with such legs, which leap rather than crawl, are allowed (verse 22).

decisions.choice: long back legs
decisions.reason: Readable explains "legs above their feet" as the long back legs used for jumping.

records.heading: Winged swarming creatures and carcasses

records.source: אֶת־אֵ֤לֶּה מֵהֶם֙ תֹּאכֵ֔לוּ אֶת־הָֽאַרְבֶּ֣ה לְמִינ֔וֹ וְאֶת־הַסָּלְעָ֖ם לְמִינֵ֑הוּ וְאֶת־הַחַרְגֹּ֣ל לְמִינֵ֔הוּ וְאֶת־הֶחָגָ֖ב לְמִינֵֽהוּ׃
records.gloss: These of them you will eat: the locust after its kind, and the bald locust after its kind, and the cricket after its kind, and the grasshopper after its kind.
pieces: Of these you may eat the following, each by its own kind: the swarming locust, the bald locust, the cricket and the grasshopper.

L.22: These of them you may eat: the locust after its kind, and the bald locust after its kind, and the cricket after its kind, and the grasshopper after its kind.

R.22: These are the ones you may eat: every kind of locust, cricket and grasshopper.

decisions.choice: locust, bald locust, cricket, grasshopper: four kinds of leaping insect
decisions.reason: All four are winged insects that leap. The first is the locust that swarms and strips the land (Exodus 10:4-15; Joel 1:4). The fourth is a grasshopper, a byword for smallness (Numbers 13:33; Isaiah 40:22). The second and third occur only here, so their names are a best guess. Eating locusts was common in the region; John the Baptist lived on locusts and wild honey (Matthew 3:4).

decisions.choice: every kind of locust, cricket and grasshopper
decisions.reason: Readable does not try to tell a young reader the difference between the locust and the bald locust, which are both locusts, and lists them together.

records.source: וְכֹל֙ שֶׁ֣רֶץ הָע֔וֹף אֲשֶׁר־ל֖וֹ אַרְבַּ֣ע רַגְלָ֑יִם שֶׁ֥קֶץ ה֖וּא לָכֶֽם׃
records.gloss: And every swarming thing of the flying [kind] which [belongs] to it four feet, detestable [is] it to you.
pieces: Every other winged swarming creature that goes on four feet is to be detestable to you.

L.23: And every swarming thing that flies that has four feet, it [is] detestable to you.

R.23: All other insects with wings that walk on their legs are disgusting to you.

decisions.choice: every swarming thing with four feet: every other winged insect, apart from those of verses 21-22
decisions.reason: The verse repeats the rule of verse 20 to close the section, with the exceptions just given. See verse 20 on "four".

decisions.choice: other
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable add "other" to show that the insects allowed in verses 21-22 are not included.

records.source: וּלְאֵ֖לֶּה תִּטַּמָּ֑אוּ כָּל־הַנֹּגֵ֥עַ בְּנִבְלָתָ֖ם יִטְמָ֥א עַד־הָעָֽרֶב׃
records.gloss: And by these you will make yourselves unclean; every [one who] touches their carcass, he will be unclean until the evening.
pieces: These too will make you unclean. Whoever touches the dead body of one of them will be unclean until evening.

L.24: And by these you will make yourselves unclean; everyone who touches their carcass shall be unclean until the evening.

R.24: Some animals will make you unclean. If you touch the body of one after it has died, you will be unclean until evening.

decisions.choice: until the evening: the uncleanness lasts until sunset, when a new day begins
decisions.reason: In Israel the day began at evening (Genesis 1:5; Leviticus 23:32), so uncleanness "until the evening" lasts for the rest of that day. It is the shortest and mildest kind of uncleanness in the law. It is often joined to washing the clothes or the body (verses 25, 28, 40; 15:5-11; 17:15), and it ends without any offering. Being unclean in this way is not a sin, but during that time the person must keep away from holy things (7:20-21; 22:4-7).

decisions.choice: by these: by the creatures named in the verses that follow
decisions.reason: "These" most naturally opens the section on uncleanness from touching dead bodies (verses 24-40), and points ahead to the animals of verses 26-28. It could also look back to the winged swarming creatures of verse 23.

decisions.choice: If you touch
decisions.reason: Readable speaks to the reader as "you", as in chapter 1, for a rule that applies to men and women alike.

records.source: וְכָל־הַנֹּשֵׂ֖א מִנִּבְלָתָ֑ם יְכַבֵּ֥ס בְּגָדָ֖יו וְטָמֵ֥א עַד־הָעָֽרֶב׃
records.gloss: And every [one who] carries [any] of their carcass, he will wash his garments and he will be unclean until the evening.
pieces: Anyone who carries any part of their dead bodies must wash their clothes, and they remain unclean until evening.

L.25: And everyone who carries [any] of their carcass shall wash his garments and be unclean until the evening.

R.25: If you carry part of a dead animal like this, you must wash your clothes. You will be unclean until evening.

decisions.choice: carries ... shall wash his garments: carrying is closer contact than touching and requires washing
decisions.reason: Someone who picks up and carries a carcass has it against their clothes, so the clothes must be washed as well. The uncleanness still lasts until evening (see verse 24).

records.source: לְֽכָל־הַבְּהֵמָ֡ה אֲשֶׁ֣ר הִוא֩ מַפְרֶ֨סֶת פַּרְסָ֜ה וְשֶׁ֣סַע׀אֵינֶ֣נָּה שֹׁסַ֗עַת וְגֵרָה֙ אֵינֶ֣נָּה מַעֲלָ֔ה טְמֵאִ֥ים הֵ֖ם לָכֶ֑ם כָּל־הַנֹּגֵ֥עַ בָּהֶ֖ם יִטְמָֽא׃
records.gloss: To every animal which it [is] dividing [a] hoof and [a] cleft not it [is] cleaving, and cud not it [is] bringing up, unclean [are] they to you; every [one who] touches them will be unclean.
pieces: Every animal with hooves that are not split all the way through, and that does not chew the cud, is unclean for you. Anyone who touches one when it is dead will become unclean.

L.26: To every animal that divides the hoof but is not split [with] a cleft, and does not bring up the cud: they [are] unclean to you; everyone who touches them shall be unclean.

R.26: Some animals have hooves that are not split all the way. They also do not chew the cud. These animals are unclean for you. If you touch one when it is dead, you will be unclean.

decisions.choice: divides the hoof but is not split with a cleft: has hooves, but not hooves split fully in two
decisions.reason: The verse describes hoofed animals that have neither of the two signs of verse 3: their hooves are not fully split, and they do not chew the cud. The horse and the donkey are examples. Whether "divides the hoof" here means a partly split hoof or simply having hooves is not clear.

decisions.choice: touches them: touches their dead bodies
decisions.reason: Verses 24, 27 and 31 speak of touching the carcass, and living donkeys were handled every day. So "them" here means these animals when dead.

decisions.choice: when it is dead
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable add "when it is dead" from the context (see the meaning decision).

records.source: וְכֹ֣ל׀הוֹלֵ֣ךְ עַל־כַּפָּ֗יו בְּכָל־הַֽחַיָּה֙ הַהֹלֶ֣כֶת עַל־אַרְבַּ֔ע טְמֵאִ֥ים הֵ֖ם לָכֶ֑ם כָּל־הַנֹּגֵ֥עַ בְּנִבְלָתָ֖ם יִטְמָ֥א עַד־הָעָֽרֶב׃
records.gloss: And any [one which] walks on its paws among every living creature which walks on four, unclean [are] they to you; every [one who] touches their carcass will be unclean until the evening.
pieces: Every four-footed creature that walks on the pads of its feet is unclean for you. Anyone who touches the carcass of one will be unclean until evening.

L.27: And everything that goes on its paws among all the living creatures that go on four [feet]: they [are] unclean to you; everyone who touches their carcass shall be unclean until the evening.

R.27: Animals with four legs that walk on paws are unclean for you. If you touch the body of one that has died, you will be unclean until evening.

decisions.choice: goes on its paws: walks on the soles of its feet, not on hooves
decisions.reason: The word means the palm of the hand or the sole of the foot. Animals that walk on padded feet, such as dogs, cats, lions and bears, have no hooves at all and are unclean.

decisions.choice: the pads of its feet
decisions.reason: Literal says "paws". Balanced says "the pads of its feet", which brings out the sense of the Hebrew word.

records.source: וְהַנֹּשֵׂא֙ אֶת־נִבְלָתָ֔ם יְכַבֵּ֥ס בְּגָדָ֖יו וְטָמֵ֣א עַד־הָעָ֑רֶב טְמֵאִ֥ים הֵ֖מָּה לָכֶֽם׃ס
records.gloss: And the [one who] carries their carcass, he will wash his garments and he will be unclean until the evening; unclean [are] they to you.
pieces: Whoever carries their carcass must wash their clothes and will be unclean until evening. These animals are unclean for you.

L.28: And the one who carries their carcass shall wash his garments and be unclean until the evening; they [are] unclean to you.

R.28: If you carry the body of one of them, you must wash your clothes. You will be unclean until evening. These animals are unclean for you.

decisions.choice: they are unclean to you: a closing summary of verses 26-28
decisions.reason: The rule for carrying is the same as in verse 25; see verse 24 on "until the evening".

records.source: וְזֶ֤ה לָכֶם֙ הַטָּמֵ֔א בַּשֶּׁ֖רֶץ הַשֹּׁרֵ֣ץ עַל־הָאָ֑רֶץ הַחֹ֥לֶד וְהָעַכְבָּ֖ר וְהַצָּ֥ב לְמִינֵֽהוּ׃
records.gloss: And this to you [is] the unclean among the swarming things which swarm on the earth: the weasel, and the mouse, and the great lizard after its kind,
pieces: Of the small creatures that swarm on the ground, these are unclean for you: the weasel, the mouse, the various kinds of great lizard,

L.29: And this [is] the unclean to you among the swarming things that swarm on the earth: the weasel, and the mouse, and the great lizard after its kind,

R.29: Some small animals that swarm on the ground are unclean for you. These are the weasel, the mouse, all kinds of large lizards,

decisions.choice: the unclean among the swarming things: eight small creatures whose dead bodies make things unclean
decisions.reason: All creatures that swarm on the ground are detestable as food (verse 41). These eight are singled out because their dead bodies make people and things unclean (verses 31-38). They are small creatures that get into houses, pots, food and water, which is the setting of the rules that follow.

decisions.choice: weasel, mouse, great lizard: probable identifications
decisions.reason: The first name has been taken as the weasel or the mole. The second is the mouse or rat (1 Samuel 6:4-5; Isaiah 66:17). The third is a large lizard, perhaps the spiny-tailed lizard of the desert; an old view took it as the tortoise.

decisions.choice: the list runs on to verse 30
decisions.reason: The list is one sentence across verses 29-30, so Literal and Balanced end verse 29 with a comma.

records.heading: Small creatures that swarm on the ground

records.source: וְהָאֲנָקָ֥ה וְהַכֹּ֖חַ וְהַלְּטָאָ֑ה וְהַחֹ֖מֶט וְהַתִּנְשָֽׁמֶת׃
records.gloss: and the gecko, and the monitor lizard, and the wall lizard, and the skink, and the chameleon.
pieces: the gecko, the monitor lizard, the wall lizard, the sand lizard and the chameleon.

L.30: and the gecko, and the monitor lizard, and the wall lizard, and the sand lizard, and the chameleon.

R.30: the gecko, the monitor lizard, the wall lizard, the sand lizard and the chameleon.

decisions.choice: gecko, monitor lizard, wall lizard, sand lizard, chameleon: probably all kinds of lizard
decisions.reason: The five names occur only here, and their identification is uncertain. The second name is the ordinary word for strength, which suits a large, strong lizard such as the monitor. The last is the same word as the bird in verse 18. Ancient versions differ, but most of the names point to lizards, which are common in houses and walls.

records.source: אֵ֛לֶּה הַטְּמֵאִ֥ים לָכֶ֖ם בְּכָל־הַשָּׁ֑רֶץ כָּל־הַנֹּגֵ֧עַ בָּהֶ֛ם בְּמֹתָ֖ם יִטְמָ֥א עַד־הָעָֽרֶב׃
records.gloss: These [are] the unclean to you among all the swarming things; every [one who] touches them in their death will be unclean until the evening.
pieces: These are the swarming creatures that are unclean for you. If anyone touches one of them once it is dead, that person will be unclean until evening.

L.31: These [are] the unclean to you among all the swarming things; everyone who touches them in their death shall be unclean until the evening.

R.31: These small animals are unclean for you. If you touch one after it has died, you will be unclean until evening.

decisions.choice: in their death: after they have died
decisions.reason: As with the larger animals, it is contact with the dead creature that makes a person unclean. See verse 24 on "until the evening".

records.source: וְכֹ֣ל אֲשֶׁר־יִפֹּל־עָלָיו֩ מֵהֶ֨ם׀בְּמֹתָ֜ם יִטְמָ֗א מִכָּל־כְּלִי־עֵץ֙ א֣וֹ בֶ֤גֶד אוֹ־עוֹר֙ א֣וֹ שָׂ֔ק כָּל־כְּלִ֕י אֲשֶׁר־יֵעָשֶׂ֥ה מְלָאכָ֖ה בָּהֶ֑ם בַּמַּ֧יִם יוּבָ֛א וְטָמֵ֥א עַד־הָעֶ֖רֶב וְטָהֵֽר׃
records.gloss: And all which falls on it [any] of them in their death will be unclean, from every vessel of wood or garment or hide or sackcloth, every vessel which work is done in them; in water it will be put, and it will be unclean until the evening, and it will be clean.
pieces: Anything that one of them falls on after it has died becomes unclean: any wooden object, any clothing, leather or sackcloth, any tool or article used for work. It must be dipped in water and will remain unclean until evening; after that it is clean.

L.32: And everything on which [any] of them falls in their death shall be unclean, any article of wood or garment or skin or sack, any article with which work is done; into water it shall be put, and it shall be unclean until the evening, and [then] it shall be clean.

R.32: Sometimes one of these dead animals may fall on something. Then that thing becomes unclean. It might be made of wood, cloth, leather or sackcloth. It might be any tool or dish that people use. Put it in water. It will be unclean until evening. After that it will be clean.

decisions.choice: article: any object made and used by people
decisions.reason: The word covers containers, tools, weapons and other equipment. Here it is any household object of wood, cloth, leather or goat-hair sackcloth that is used for work.

decisions.choice: into water it shall be put: washing makes the object clean again at evening
decisions.reason: Objects that can be washed are made clean by water and the passing of the day, as people are (verse 25). Pottery, which cannot be washed clean, is treated differently (verse 33).

records.source: וְכָל־כְּלִי־חֶ֔רֶשׂ אֲשֶׁר־יִפֹּ֥ל מֵהֶ֖ם אֶל־תּוֹכ֑וֹ כֹּ֣ל אֲשֶׁ֧ר בְּתוֹכ֛וֹ יִטְמָ֖א וְאֹת֥וֹ תִשְׁבֹּֽרוּ׃
records.gloss: And every vessel of earthenware which falls [any] of them into its middle, all which [is] in its midst will be unclean, and it you will break.
pieces: If one of them falls inside a pot made of clay, all that is in the pot becomes unclean, and the pot itself must be smashed.

L.33: And every earthenware vessel into whose midst [any] of them falls, all that [is] in its midst shall be unclean, and it you shall break.

R.33: Suppose one falls into a clay pot. Then all that is inside becomes unclean, and the pot must be broken.

decisions.choice: earthenware vessel ... you shall break: a clay pot cannot be made clean, so it is destroyed
decisions.reason: Unglazed clay soaks up what touches it. The law does not let it be washed clean like wood or cloth, so it must be broken. The same is required of a clay pot in which a sin offering has been boiled (6:21) and one touched by a man with a discharge (15:12).

records.source: מִכָּל־הָאֹ֜כֶל אֲשֶׁ֣ר יֵאָכֵ֗ל אֲשֶׁ֨ר יָב֥וֹא עָלָ֛יו מַ֖יִם יִטְמָ֑א וְכָל־מַשְׁקֶה֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר יִשָּׁתֶ֔ה בְּכָל־כְּלִ֖י יִטְמָֽא׃
records.gloss: From all the food which may be eaten, which comes on it water, will be unclean, and every drink which is drunk in every vessel will be unclean.
pieces: Any food that could be eaten becomes unclean if water from such a pot has come on it, and any drink in such a pot becomes unclean.

L.34: Of all the food that may be eaten, on which water comes, it shall be unclean; and any drink that may be drunk in any vessel shall be unclean.

R.34: Food that has had water from that pot on it is unclean. So is anything to drink that was in that pot.

decisions.choice: on which water comes ... in any vessel: food and drink in the unclean pot of verse 33
alternatives: any moist food anywhere becomes unclean if the creature touches it
decisions.reason: The verse goes on from the clay pot of verse 33: food wetted with water from it, and drink in it, become unclean. Verse 38 shows that something wet takes on uncleanness more readily than something dry, so the verse may also state a wider rule about moist food.

decisions.choice: from such a pot / that pot
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable link the water and the drink to the pot of verse 33, as the context implies.

records.source: וְ֠כֹל אֲשֶׁר־יִפֹּ֨ל מִנִּבְלָתָ֥ם׀עָלָיו֮ יִטְמָא֒ תַּנּ֧וּר וְכִירַ֛יִם יֻתָּ֖ץ טְמֵאִ֣ים הֵ֑ם וּטְמֵאִ֖ים יִהְי֥וּ לָכֶֽם׃
records.gloss: And all which falls [any] of their carcass on it will be unclean; [an] oven and [a] stove will be broken down; unclean [are] they, and unclean they will be to you.
pieces: Anything touched by part of their carcass when it falls becomes unclean. If it is an oven or a stove, it must be torn down. These are unclean, and you are to keep treating them as unclean.

L.35: And everything on which [any] of their carcass falls shall be unclean; an oven or a stove shall be broken down; they [are] unclean, and unclean they shall be to you.

R.35: If part of one of these dead animals falls on anything, it becomes unclean. If it is an oven or a stove, you must break it into pieces. It is unclean, and you must treat it as unclean.

decisions.choice: oven and stove: fixed cooking places made of clay, which must be broken up
decisions.reason: The oven was a clay cylinder heated from inside, used for baking bread (2:4). The second word is a pair of supports of clay or stone over a fire, on which a pot was set. Being made of clay, they are treated like the pot of verse 33 and broken down.

records.source: אַ֣ךְ מַעְיָ֥ן וּב֛וֹר מִקְוֵה־מַ֖יִם יִהְיֶ֣ה טָה֑וֹר וְנֹגֵ֥עַ בְּנִבְלָתָ֖ם יִטְמָֽא׃
records.gloss: Nevertheless [a] spring and [a] cistern, [a] collecting place of water, will be clean; and [the one who] touches their carcass will be unclean.
pieces: Water in a spring or a cistern, where water is gathered, stays clean. But whoever touches the carcass will be unclean.

L.36: Nevertheless, a spring or a cistern, a gathering of water, shall be clean; but the one who touches their carcass shall be unclean.

R.36: But a spring or a well where water collects stays clean. Still, if you touch the dead animal in it, you become unclean.

decisions.choice: a spring or a cistern, a gathering of water: a water supply stays clean even if a carcass falls into it

decisions.reason: The three phrases cover every way a small ground creature moves: with no legs, with four, and with many.

pieces: For I am {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} your God. Consecrate yourselves, then. You must be holy, because I am holy. None of the creatures that creep on the ground must make you unclean.

L.44: For I [am] {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} your God, and you shall consecrate yourselves, and you will be holy, for holy [am] I. And you shall not make yourselves unclean by any swarming thing that creeps on the earth.

R.44: I am {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} your God. Set yourselves apart as holy. You must be holy, because I am holy. Do not let any animal that creeps on the ground make you unclean.

decisions.choice: be holy, for I am holy: Israel is to be set apart for God and to share his character
alternatives: you will be holy, for I am holy (a promise)
decisions.reason: To be holy is to be set apart as belonging to God, and so to be unlike what is common or unclean. The reason given is God himself: he is holy, and his people must be like him. This is the first time Leviticus says it; it returns as the heart of the laws for daily life (19:2; 20:7, 26). Here it is tied to food: what Israel eats marks it out as God's people, just as God set Israel apart from the nations (20:24-26; Exodus 19:6). The verb form can also be read as a promise, "you will be holy", but with the commands around it, it is a command.

decisions.choice: quoted in the New Testament: 1 Peter 1:15-16
decisions.reason: Peter quotes these words, "Be holy, because I am holy", to call followers of Jesus to holy living in all their conduct. The words are found in 11:44-45, 19:2 and 20:7.

decisions.choice: consecrate yourselves: set yourselves apart as holy
decisions.reason: The reflexive verb means to make oneself holy, here by keeping away from what is unclean. See 8:10.

decisions.reason: Readable uses the settled Readable wording for "consecrate".
